lesson.title: Channel Capacity: The Speed Limit Built Into the Wire
lesson.summary: Channel capacity is the theoretical maximum data rate a communication channel can carry, a limit set jointly by the channel's bandwidth and its signal characteristics, long before noise gets factored into the picture.
lesson.body:
Every communication channel, a length of copper, a fiber strand, a slice of radio spectrum, has a bandwidth: a range of frequencies it can carry effectively, measured in hertz. Bandwidth is not just an abstract number; it directly limits how quickly a signal can change state, because a channel that only passes a narrow range of frequencies physically cannot support very rapid transitions between signal levels without distorting them beyond recognition. Channel capacity formalizes this relationship into a maximum data rate: the largest number of bits per second that a given channel, with its own particular bandwidth and signal characteristics, can theoretically deliver.

The earliest formal version of this idea, developed by Harry Nyquist well before information theory existed as a field, considers a channel with no noise at all and asks how fast it can transmit given only its bandwidth and how many distinguishable signal levels are used per symbol. Nyquist's result is that the maximum symbol rate a channel of bandwidth B, in hertz, can support is 2B symbols per second, and if each symbol is drawn from M distinguishable levels, the maximum noiseless data rate becomes C equals 2B times log2(M) bits per second. This formula ties directly back to the symbol rate and modulation ideas from earlier chapters: bandwidth caps the symbol rate, and the number of distinguishable levels per symbol determines how many bits each symbol carries, exactly the log2(M) relationship you already saw connecting symbol rate to bit rate.

Work through a concrete case: a channel with 3000 Hz of usable bandwidth, roughly the range a traditional telephone line carries, using an 8 level signal so each symbol encodes log2(8), or 3, bits. Nyquist's formula gives a maximum noiseless capacity of 2 times 3000 times 3, or 18,000 bits per second. Push the level count higher and the noiseless capacity keeps climbing without any obvious ceiling, since log2(M) grows without bound as M grows, which is exactly the gap that makes Nyquist's formula incomplete on its own: in the real world you cannot keep adding signal levels forever, because noise on the channel eventually makes adjacent levels impossible to tell apart.

That gap is precisely what the Shannon theorem, covered next, closes. Nyquist's formula answers how many symbols per second a channel's bandwidth allows and how capacity would scale if you could always add more distinguishable levels; it says nothing about how many levels a real, noisy channel can actually support before a receiver starts confusing one level for another. Channel capacity as a concept, then, is really two contributions layered together: a bandwidth driven ceiling on symbol rate that Nyquist worked out first, and a noise driven ceiling on how many levels each symbol can safely carry, which required a later and more general treatment to pin down.
